description: Pointers, addresses, pointer arithmetic and pointers with arrays and functions in C

questions.questionText: What is a pointer in C?
questions.optionA: A variable that stores another variable's value only
questions.optionB: A variable that stores the address of another variable
questions.explanation: A pointer variable stores the memory address of another variable.

questions.questionText: Which operator is used to get the address of a variable?
questions.explanation: The address-of operator & gives the memory address of a variable.

questions.questionText: Which operator is used to access the value stored at the address held by a pointer?
questions.explanation: The * operator is used for dereferencing a pointer.

questions.questionText: Which is the correct declaration of a pointer to an integer?
questions.explanation: int *p declares p as a pointer to an integer.

questions.questionText: What will be the output? int x = 10; int *p = &x; printf("%d", *p);
questions.explanation: p stores the address of x, so *p gives the value stored in x, which is 10.

questions.questionText: What will be the output? int x = 10; int *p = &x; *p = 20; printf("%d", x);
questions.explanation: Changing *p changes the value of x because p points to x.

questions.questionText: What does a NULL pointer represent?
questions.optionA: A pointer pointing to the first variable
questions.optionB: A pointer that does not point to a valid object or function
questions.optionC: A pointer containing zero as a valid object address
questions.explanation: A null pointer represents a pointer that is not pointing to a valid object or function.

questions.questionText: Which header file defines the NULL macro in standard C implementations?
questions.optionC: Both can provide it through standard headers
questions.explanation: NULL is defined by several standard headers, including stdio.h and stdlib.h.

questions.questionText: What will be the output? int x = 5; int *p = &x; printf("%d", *(&x));
questions.explanation: &x gives the address of x and dereferencing it with * gives the value 5.

questions.questionText: If int x = 10; what does &x represent?
questions.explanation: The & operator returns the memory address of the variable x.

questions.questionText: What is pointer arithmetic?
questions.optionA: Performing arithmetic on the pointer address according to the pointed-to type
questions.optionD: Converting a pointer to a string
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic allows operations such as incrementing or decrementing a pointer based on the size of its pointed-to type.

questions.questionText: If p is an int pointer, what does p + 1 generally point to?
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the size of the pointed-to type, so p + 1 points to the next int element when used with an int array.

questions.questionText: What will be the output? int a[] = {10, 20, 30}; int *p = a; printf("%d", *(p + 1));
questions.explanation: p points to a[0], so *(p + 1) accesses a[1], which is 20.

questions.questionText: In most expressions, the name of an array represents:
questions.optionB: A pointer to its first element
questions.optionD: A pointer to its last element
questions.explanation: Except in contexts such as sizeof and &, an array name generally converts to a pointer to its first element.

questions.questionText: What is the relationship between arr[i] and *(arr + i)?
questions.optionC: arr[i] is a pointer but *(arr+i) is an integer
questions.explanation: The C language defines array subscripting so that arr[i] is equivalent to *(arr + i).

questions.questionText: Which type of pointer can hold the address of an object of any object type?
questions.explanation: A void pointer can hold the address of an object of any object type and is commonly used for generic programming.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a pointer to pointer?
questions.optionB: To store the address of another pointer
questions.explanation: A pointer to pointer stores the address of another pointer variable.

questions.questionText: Which is the correct declaration of a pointer to a pointer to int?
questions.explanation: int **p declares p as a pointer to a pointer to int.

questions.questionText: What will be the output? int x = 10; int *p = &x; int **q = &p; printf("%d", **q);
questions.explanation: q points to p and *q gives p. Therefore **q gives the value of x, which is 10.

questions.questionText: How can a function modify the original variable passed from the caller?
questions.optionB: By passing its address using a pointer
questions.optionC: By using a local variable only
questions.explanation: Passing the address of a variable allows the function to modify the original variable through dereferencing.

questions.questionText: What will be the output? void change(int *p) { *p = 50; } int main() { int x = 10; change(&x); printf("%d", x); }
questions.explanation: The address of x is passed to change(), so *p refers to x and changes its value to 50.

questions.questionText: Which pointer operation is generally valid when p and q point into the same array?
questions.explanation: Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of elements between them, subject to the rules of pointer arithmetic.

questions.questionText: What is a dangling pointer?
questions.optionA: A pointer that points to valid memory
questions.optionB: A pointer that points to an object whose lifetime has ended
questions.explanation: A dangling pointer refers to memory that is no longer a valid object, for example after the pointed-to object's lifetime ends.

questions.questionText: What will happen if a pointer is dereferenced when it does not point to a valid object?
questions.explanation: Dereferencing an invalid pointer results in undefined behavior.

questions.questionText: What will be the output? int a = 10, b = 20; int *p = &a; int *q = &b; *p = *p + *q; printf("%d", a);
questions.explanation: *p refers to a and *q refers to b. Therefore a becomes 10 + 20 = 30.
